chapter_title: Parallelism and Concurrency for Game Engines

screens.title: Parallelism and Concurrency for Game Engines
screens.subtitle: Why multi-core programming is essential for modern games

narration.text: Modern game engines must complete many computations every frame: physics, rendering, AI, asset streaming, input, and network work. Relying on a single C P U core no longer meets the performance demands of contemporary games. In this lesson you will learn how concurrency and parallelism differ, why parallelism matters for frame rate and responsiveness, and which C++ tools help you safely split work across cores. We will ground ideas with concrete examples such as processing thousands of particles in parallel, protecting shared resources like an asset cache with mutexes, and simplifying task management with async and futures. You will also see common pitfalls — race conditions, deadlocks, and livelocks — and simple patterns to avoid them. By the end of the chapter you will understand when to create raw threads, when to prefer task-based APIs, and how to reason about shared data. Think of this as learning how to coordinate many cooks in a kitchen so each can contribute without interfering with the others. As you explore the topic, notice the trade-offs between control and complexity and prepare to practice with the provided starter code that parallelizes agent updates.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Parallelism uses multiple cores to run tasks at the same time; concurrency manages multiple tasks that may run overlapping in time. Both are essential to scale game engine performance, but they require careful synchronization.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives guide our work through parallelism and concurrency in a game engine context. First, you'll understand the fundamental difference between concurrency and parallelism: concurrency is about managing multiple tasks, while parallelism is about running tasks simultaneously on multiple cores. Second, you will be able to identify engine subsystems that benefit from multi-threading, such as rendering, physics, AI, and background asset loading. Third, you will implement basic multi-threading using the C++ standard's thread class, launching work, and ensuring proper lifetime with join or detach. Fourth, you will protect shared state using mutexes and RAII wrappers like lock_guard to prevent race conditions. Each objective includes a concrete example: for instance, using threads to process chunks of particle data, or protecting an asset cache map during concurrent insertions. You will also practice reading and reasoning about simple code snippets that show thread creation, synchronization, and task-based futures. Finally, expect to contrast common mistakes with correct patterns so you can recognize deadlocks or unsafe sharing in code. These skills make real performance improvements safer and more maintainable in your engine.

keyIdea.text: Be able to parallelize independent work and protect shared resources so behavior is deterministic and safe.

screens.subtitle: Apply core C++ concurrency APIs safely

narration.text: Beyond objectives, you'll gain practical coding skills. You will write small parallel loops using std::thread and chunking strategies to distribute work across cores. You will practice passing references safely to threads, understanding that std::thread copies arguments by default and std::ref is used to pass references. You will implement synchronization via std::mutex and std::lock_guard to protect shared counters, logs, or asset caches. You will reason about deadlocks and learn simple avoidance techniques such as consistent lock ordering. Finally, you'll explore std::async and std::future to implement task-based parallelism where results are needed later. For example, you might launch asynchronous calls to compute partial sums across a large data buffer and then combine the futures, which simplifies thread lifetime management. Each objective includes a mnemonic or mini-diagram to link the idea to common engine systems and a verified competency milestone to mark readiness. These skills prioritize both performance and safety, two pillars of robust game engine code.

screens.title: Concurrency vs. Parallelism
screens.subtitle: Clear definitions and a chef analogy

narration.text: Start with two precise definitions. Concurrency is the property of a system that can make progress on multiple tasks by interleaving their execution. Parallelism is the property of executing multiple tasks at the same time on different processing units. In game development we often use concurrency language loosely, but the practical target is parallelism: we want physics, AI, and rendering work to run simultaneously on separate cores to finish a frame faster. A helpful analogy: a single chef handling multiple orders by switching between them is concurrency; multiple chefs each preparing an order at the same time is parallelism. Concrete example: updating 10,000 independent particles can be parallelized by splitting particles into chunks and processing each chunk on a different core. A common misconception is that concurrency automatically gives you faster execution. It doesn't — concurrency can help responsiveness on a single core, but true speed-up comes from parallelism on multiple cores. Key takeaway: reason about your problem's dependencies. If work units are independent, aim for parallelism. If they share state or require ordered access, concurrency management and synchronization are necessary to avoid incorrect results. Ask yourself: can this task run without accessing shared mutable data? If yes, it's a good candidate for parallel execution.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Concurrency manages multiple tasks; parallelism runs them simultaneously. Aim for parallelism in multi-core game engines where tasks are independent.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Concurrency vs Parallelism
Definitions
Precise meanings and practical implications for engine work.
Concurrency
Managing multiple tasks which may be interleaved or overlap in time; useful for responsiveness.
Parallelism
Executing tasks at the same time on multiple CPU cores to reduce wall-clock time.
Chef analogy
One chef switching tasks is concurrency; multiple chefs cooking simultaneously is parallelism. Which do you want for per-frame updates? Usually parallelism.
Practical checklist
  • Identify independent work units. If none, avoid heavy parallelization.
  • Prefer parallelism for large batches like particles or rigid body updates.
  • Use concurrency to manage I/O, asset streaming, and responsiveness.
Concrete example
Split 10,000 particles into 4 chunks and process each chunk on a separate thread to reduce per-frame compute time.
Key Takeaway

Parallelism gives real speed-up on multi-core hardware; concurrency helps manage many tasks but is not always faster.

screens.title: Parallelizable Engine Tasks
screens.subtitle: Which engine systems benefit and how to partition work

narration.text: When deciding what to parallelize, start by listing independent work. Common engine systems that benefit are particle systems, physics updates for independent rigid bodies, AI behaviors for many NPCs, and background asset decompression or loading. The process is: identify independence, partition the data into chunks, schedule each chunk to a worker (thread or task), and finally synchronize results if they must be combined before render. For example, for physics you can divide bodies by spatial regions so each thread updates bodies in a different region. For AI you can assign groups of NPCs to different worker tasks. A common partitioning strategy is chunking: split a large array into N contiguous ranges and let each worker operate on its range. One misconception is that smaller chunks always yield better scaling — too-small chunks increase scheduling overhead and reduce cache locality. Another is assuming writes to different objects are automatically safe; if other systems read or write the same objects concurrently, you must ensure proper ordering or locks. Practical hint: measure and profile. Start with a coarse partition, then refine based on hotspots. The closing question: for your game, which subsystem has the most independent work you can safely parallelize?

keyIdea.title: Partition pattern
keyIdea.text: Partition independent work into chunks per thread and measure; avoid tiny chunks that hurt performance.

narration.text: Let's walk through a canonical chunk-processing example that uses std::thread. The approach is simple: divide a large vector into chunks, create a thread per chunk, and then join all threads. Important details include passing large containers by reference using std::ref because std::thread copies arguments by default. Also, remember to call join on each thread to avoid premature program termination; an unjoined std::thread destructor will call terminate. Concrete example: double values across a large vector by splitting it into four ranges and launching four threads that each call processChunk with start and end indices. A common misconception is that creating many threads is always better. Thread creation and teardown have overhead, so match the number of threads to hardware or use a thread pool. Another pitfall is forgetting to handle uneven chunk sizes for the last thread — handle the remainder explicitly. Finally, always consider whether tasks actually write to shared memory; if they do, synchronization is required. Takeaway: std::thread gives explicit control but requires careful argument passing and lifetime management. Practice by compiling and observing that the printed finished messages appear for each thread and that data changes as expected.

keyIdea.title: Thread pattern
keyIdea.text: Use std::thread to run chunked work, pass containers by std::ref, and join all threads to ensure deterministic completion.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › std::thread Example
Code
<!-- Escaped C++ example -->
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>
#include <numeric>

void processChunk(std::vector<int>& data, int start, int end) {
  for (int i = start; i < end; ++i) {
    data[i] *= 2; // simulate heavy computation
  }
  std::cout << "Thread processing chunk [" << start << ", " << end << ") finished." << std::endl;
}

int main() {
  std::vector<int> gameData(10000);
  std::iota(gameData.begin(), gameData.end(), 1);

  const int numThreads = 4;
  std::vector<std::thread> threads;
  int chunkSize = gameData.size() / numThreads;

  for (int i = 0; i < numThreads; ++i) {
    int start = i * chunkSize;
    int end = (i == numThreads - 1) ? gameData.size() : (i + 1) * chunkSize;
    threads.emplace_back(processChunk, std::ref(gameData), start, end);
  }

  for (auto & t : threads) t.join();
  return 0;
}
Explanation
  • std::thread starts a new execution context when constructed with a callable.
  • Arguments are copied by default; use std::ref to pass references to large containers.
  • Always join threads to ensure they finish and to avoid std::terminate on destruction.
Concrete example
Doubling 10,000 integers in four parallel chunks reduces wall-clock time compared to a single-threaded loop on multi-core hardware.
Key Takeaway

Raw threads give control but require careful argument passing and lifetime management. Profile thread count to match hardware.

screens.title: Shared Data and Race Conditions
screens.subtitle: Why simultaneous access can break correctness

narration.text: Race conditions occur when multiple threads access the same memory location and at least one of the accesses is a write, and the final result depends on the timing of those accesses. They are nondeterministic and often hard to reproduce. A concrete example from the chapter is multiple threads incrementing a shared counter without synchronization. Each increment appears atomic in source code but can be multiple machine instructions that interleave, causing lost updates. To reason about correctness, ask whether any two threads could write the same variable concurrently. If yes, you have a data race. Another misconception is that printf or console output will make access safe — it does not; console input and output itself may be non-atomic and can interleave messages. The fix is to use a mutex to guard the critical section. Prefer std::lock_guard because it acquires the lock on construction and releases it on scope exit, ensuring exception safety. Takeaway: identify critical sections that mutate shared data, wrap them with mutex protection, and keep locked sections small to reduce contention. A closing reflection: which variables in your systems are written by multiple threads, and how would you minimize the locked region to preserve parallel throughput?

keyIdea.title: Race condition
keyIdea.text: A race occurs when unsynchronized concurrent writes lead to unpredictable final state; protect critical sections with mutexes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Race Conditions
Problem
Shared mutable state without synchronization leads to unpredictable results.
// Illustration: incrementing a shared counter
int sharedCounter = 0;
void incrementCounter(int &counter) {
  for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) {
    counter++; // not atomic — race condition if multiple threads run this
  }
}
Solution
#include <mutex>
std::mutex mtx;
void incrementCounter(int &counter) {
  for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) {
    std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(mtx);
    counter++;
  }
}
Keep the locked region as small as possible to reduce blocking; locking too broadly kills parallelism.
Key Takeaway

Identify writes to shared memory, protect them with mutexes, and keep critical sections minimal to preserve throughput.

screens.title: std::mutex and std::lock_guard in practice
screens.subtitle: Protect console logging and shared caches safely

narration.text: std::mutex is the fundamental primitive for mutual exclusion. Use it to protect critical sections such as updating a shared counter, writing to a shared asset cache, or serializing console output. The chapter demonstrates a thread-safe logging function that locks a global console mutex, writes the message, and then unlocks. Prefer std::lock_guard because it follows RAII: it acquires the lock on construction and releases on destruction, even if an exception is thrown. A concrete example: implement logMessage that takes a string, constructs a lock_guard on the console mutex, and then performs the console write. Avoid common mistakes: calling lock then performing multiple operations that could block long — keep the locked region short. Also avoid locking several mutexes in arbitrary order; this leads to deadlocks. Instead, adopt a consistent lock acquisition order across your codebase. Finally, understand that mutexes are not a cure-all: they serialize access and can reduce parallelism if overused. The takeaway is to protect only truly shared mutable state and use RAII wrappers like lock_guard for safety and clarity. std::mutex and std::lock_guard in practice means use std::mutex to guard shared resources and std::lock_guard for exception-safe locking and unlocking.. In practical terms, protect console logging and shared caches safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Mutex pattern
keyIdea.text: Use std::mutex to guard shared resources and std::lock_guard for exception-safe locking and unlocking.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › std::mutex & lock_guard
Thread-safe logging
#include <mutex>
#include <iostream>

std::mutex consoleMutex;

void logMessage(const std::string & message) {
  std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(consoleMutex);
  std::cout << message << std::endl;
}
Locking the console prevents interleaved output that can be hard to read and debug.
Guidelines
  • Keep critical sections small and fast to reduce contention.
  • Prefer scoped locks like std::lock_guard to avoid forgetting unlocks.
  • For multiple mutexes, use consistent acquisition order to avoid deadlocks.
Concrete scenario
Multiple worker threads update an AssetCache. Wrap insert and erase operations with a mutex to prevent map corruption.
Key Takeaway

Use mutexes for correctness; design your data access patterns to minimize the amount of time locks are held.

screens.title: Deadlocks, Livelocks, and Starvation
screens.subtitle: Recognize, contrast, and prevent common concurrency hazards

narration.text: Beyond races, three other concurrency hazards deserve attention. Deadlock occurs when two or more threads wait indefinitely for resources held by each other. A classic example is thread A locked mutex1 and then attempts to lock mutex2, while thread B locks mutex2 then attempts to lock mutex1; both block forever. The primary prevention technique is a consistent locking order: always acquire locks in a globally agreed sequence. Livelock is when threads are not blocked but keep changing state in response to each other without making progress — for example two threads repeatedly yielding to each other to avoid conflict. Livelock needs back-off strategies or redesign to break the reactive loop. Starvation happens when a thread rarely or never gets C P U or resource access because others monopolize it; fairness mechanisms or redesign can avoid this. A common misconception is that adding locks will always make things safe; locks can introduce deadlock or reduce throughput. Practical advice: prefer coarse patterns like task-based parallelism when possible, keep lock scope minimal, and document lock order for any code that acquires multiple mutexes. Ask yourself: could two locks be acquired in different orders anywhere in this subsystem? If yes, refactor to a single ordered acquisition.

keyIdea.title: Hazard summary
keyIdea.text: Deadlock blocks threads forever; livelock prevents progress through reactive loops; starvation denies a thread access to resources.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Deadlocks & Hazards
Deadlock
Two or more threads wait forever for resources held by each other. Prevent with consistent lock ordering.
Livelock
Threads continuously change state in response to others but make no progress. Use back-off strategies or redesign to break cycles.
Starvation
A thread rarely gets CPU or resources because others dominate. Introduce fairness or adjust scheduling.
Concrete advice
  • Document global lock ordering and always acquire locks in that order.
  • Reduce the number of locks held simultaneously by redesigning shared data structures.
  • Prefer task-based APIs to avoid manual lock management when possible.

narration.text: std::async and std::future provide a higher-level approach to parallelism. Instead of explicitly creating threads, you call std::async with a callable and receive a future that will hold the result. This abstracts thread creation and scheduling, and is a natural fit for tasks that return values, such as partial sums. A concrete example from the chapter splits a large vector into chunks and uses std::async with std::launch::async to hint at new threads, returning futures for each chunk’s sum. Later, calling get on each future blocks until that result is ready, and then you combine the partial sums. A common misconception is that std::async always creates a new thread; it is implementation-defined unless you specify the launch policy, so prefer std::launch::async if you want a new thread. Another advantage is simplified lifetime management: you do not manually join threads. However, futures that never get waited on can still consume resources, so manage them carefully. The takeaway: std::async is great for task-based problems where you need results; it reduces bookkeeping compared to raw threads while remaining explicit enough for careful control. std::async and std::future means use std::async and std::future to launch tasks and retrieve results, simplifying thread management for value-returning work.. In practical terms, task-based parallelism and retrieving results. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Task-based API
keyIdea.text: Use std::async and std::future to launch tasks and retrieve results, simplifying thread management for value-returning work.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › std::async & future
Code
#include <future>
#include <vector>
#include <numeric>

long long sumRange(const std::vector<int>& data, int start, int end) {
  long long total = 0;
  for (int i = start; i < end; ++i) total += data[i];
  return total;
}

// launch async tasks, collect futures, and combine results with .get()
Explanation
  • std::async launches a callable and returns a std::future for its result.
  • Call future.get() to wait for completion and retrieve the value.
  • Prefer std::launch::async when you want a new thread rather than deferred execution.
Concrete example
Compute partial sums with async calls, then combine futures to produce the total sum without manual join bookkeeping.
Key Takeaway

std::async simplifies task-based parallelism and result aggregation, often safer than managing many raw threads.

screens.title: Designing for Maintainable Concurrency
screens.subtitle: Patterns that reduce bugs and keep performance scalable

narration.text: Design choices determine how maintainable and efficient your concurrent code will be. Favor task-based designs where possible: define units of work, submit them to a pool or use std::async, and collect results. Keep lock scope minimal and document any global lock ordering rules. Use immutable data or thread-local storage where it makes sense to avoid locks entirely. When using mutexes, prefer RAII wrappers and consider read–write locks or fine-grained locking for hot reads with rare writes. Measure and profile to discover contention; adding more threads does not always help when locks are saturated. Another pattern is to separate data ownership: have a dedicated worker own a set of objects and only expose thread-safe messages to request updates, which avoids frequent locking. Misconception to avoid: assuming that moving code into a new thread automatically improves performance. Always measure per-frame timing and consider cache behavior. The final question: which of these patterns maps best to your engine’s architecture — thread pool with job queue, per-system worker ownership, or async tasks for ad-hoc computations? Designing for Maintainable Concurrency means prefer task-based systems, keep locks small, use ownership or immutability to avoid heavy synchronization, and always profile.. In practical terms, patterns that reduce bugs and keep performance scalable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Prefer task-based systems, keep locks small, use ownership or immutability to avoid heavy synchronization, and always profile.

Patterns
Thread pool / job queue
Submit small tasks to a shared pool to avoid frequent thread creation.
Owner-per-system
Give ownership of data to a single worker and communicate via messages to reduce locking.
Immutable snapshots
Snapshot data for read-only tasks to avoid synchronization on reads.
Async tasks
Use std::async for ad-hoc computations that return values.
Checklist
  • Profile first, parallelize hot independent work.
  • Document lock ordering and keep locks brief.
  • Prefer ownership or immutable data to reduce contention.
Key Takeaway

Good architecture reduces the need for locks and scales better than ad-hoc threading changes.

screens.title: Raw Threads vs Task-based APIs
screens.subtitle: Compare control, complexity, and correctness trade-offs

narration.text: Choosing between raw std::thread and task-based APIs like std::async is a question of trade-offs. Raw threads give you explicit control over thread lifetime, affinity, and scheduling, which can be necessary for specialized engine subsystems. However, manual thread management increases complexity: you must manage argument passing, join/detach choices, and lifetime to avoid terminate calls. Task-based APIs abstract thread management. std::async returns a future and reduces bookkeeping when you only care about results. It often integrates better with a thread pool and improves code clarity. A concrete scenario: for per-frame chunk processing where you simply need to run independent jobs and combine results, std::async reduces error surface. For a long-running worker dedicated to a subsystem with affinity needs, a raw thread may be better. Misconception: that task-based APIs are always slower — not necessarily; they can use pools and avoid frequent thread creation. Key takeaway: prefer higher-level task abstractions for typical parallel workloads and reserve raw threads for cases that require precise control and tuning. The reflective question: which approach simplifies reasoning about correctness for your feature while still meeting performance goals?

keyIdea.title: Trade-off
keyIdea.text: Use task-based APIs for simpler, result-oriented tasks; use raw threads when you need fine-grained control and tuning.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Threads vs Tasks
Raw std::thread
  • Full control over thread lifecycle and affinity.
  • Requires explicit join/detach and careful argument passing.
  • Higher risk of lifecycle bugs if not managed correctly.
std::async / std::future
  • Simplifies task submission and result retrieval.
  • Reduces bookkeeping and often plays well with thread pools.
  • Use std::launch::async to request immediate execution on a new thread.
Example decision

If you need values returned and want less management, choose async. If you need a dedicated long-running thread with special scheduling, choose std::thread.

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential terms you should keep front of mind. Concurrency is about managing multiple tasks that may overlap in time, while parallelism is executing multiple tasks simultaneously on separate cores. std::thread is the basic building block to spawn threads, and you must join them or detach them responsibly. Race conditions happen when threads access shared data without synchronization. Use std::mutex and std::lock_guard to protect critical sections and prefer RAII for safety. Deadlocks arise when different threads acquire locks in inconsistent orders; prevent them with a global lock ordering. std::async and std::future provide a task-based model to launch work and retrieve results without explicit thread management. These concepts form the toolbox for building multi-threaded game engine systems. Keep this checklist handy when you design or debug parallel code: identify independence, partition work, protect shared state, keep locks small, and profile your changes. Which concept will you apply first in your engine?

keyIdea.title: Summary
keyIdea.text: Identify independent work, use appropriate C++ primitives, and protect shared resources to build safe, scalable parallel systems.

std::thread
Creates a new thread; remember to join or detach to manage lifetime.
std::mutex & lock_guard

Takeaway
Parallelism improves performance when work is independent; synchronization ensures correctness. Use the right abstraction for the job and measure the results.
